parts: The Internet ('Net') is a global network of networks that lets anyone with a device and a connection communicate across the world. An intranet is a private network designed for a particular group of people, such as the employees of a company, who are given a user id and password; it is not open to the public. In simple terms the internet is a public space and an intranet a private space.

Requirements: a digital device (computer or laptop) with a web browser, a modem or router and an account with an Internet Service Provider (ISP). A modem (Modulator-Demodulator) converts a digital signal into an analog signal for telephone lines (modulation) and analog back into digital (demodulation); it links the device and the ISP. An ISP is a company that offers internet services for a fee (MTNL, BSNL). When connecting, the user id and password are checked. A web browser is software for viewing web pages; a web page is a document written in HTML (Hypertext Markup Language); the World Wide Web (www) is the collection of billions of web pages on connected computers.

Wired versus wireless: wired connections are cheaper to install, more secure and have a steady signal but the workstations are fixed and installation becomes difficult as computers increase; wireless installation is easy and flexible within the range of the access point, but costs more (adaptors, access points), has limited and varying signal strength and is less secure because signals can be intercepted. Wired examples: dial-up (modem dials the ISP's number over a landline; cheap and slow; phone and internet cannot be used together), DSL (Digital Subscriber Line; two lines, 'Always On', 128 Kbps to 50 Mbps) and cable connection (cable modem over cable TV lines, 512 Kbps to 100 Mbps). Wireless examples: satellite (10 to 50 Mbps), Wi-Fi (Wireless Fidelity; local area network using high-frequency radio signals or infrared over short distances at homes, hotels, malls and airports) and WiMax (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access; very high speed, radio signals or microwaves, range up to 30 miles or about 50 km).

Mobile connections: a mobile phone accesses the internet through cellular towers or through wireless modems (Wi-Fi/WiMax). 2G carried text data only; 3G raised speed up to 200 kbps and brought video calls and GPS; 4G offers up to 100 Mbps for mobile users and 1 Gbps for fixed users, enabling high-quality audio/video, gaming, HD mobile TV and cloud computing.
Surfing the net and how the internet works

The www works on client-server architecture: the computer is the client that sends a request, a web address typed in the address bar, to the server of the ISP, which returns the page; hyperlinks connect pages, and moving from page to page is called surfing the net. Each computer has a unique IP address. Rules for transferring data are called protocols; the two most important are TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol). TCP breaks the data into fixed-size packets, IP gives each packet the IP addresses of the sender and receiver, the packets travel from network to network, and TCP reassembles them at the destination; lost or garbled packets are requested again.

A web browser is software that reads and interprets HTML documents on the www; examples are Internet Explorer, Mozilla Firefox, Safari and Google Chrome. Features: address bar (type the address and click Go or press Enter); navigation buttons – Back (previous page), Forward (next page), Refresh (reloads the page from the server), Stop (stops downloading) and Home (opens the home page); Favourites/Bookmarks (store frequently visited pages in folders); History (recently visited pages, by default saved for 20 days, sortable by date, site name or visits); Tools (save, print, view a page). Internet Explorer: by Microsoft, free with Windows, first released with Windows 95 in 1995. Mozilla Firefox: free, open source, by Mozilla Corporation, released in 2002, for Windows, MacOS and Linux. Google Chrome: by Google Inc., released in 2008; it has a 'Customize and Control Google Chrome' button instead of Home, Favourites and History buttons.

A search engine is a tool (a set of programs) that finds information on the web; examples are Google, Bing, Yahoo! and MSN Search. Keywords or phrases are entered in the search box or address bar; the search engine sends a spider to retrieve matching pages, images, audio or video, and the list shown is the Search Engine Results Page (SERP).

Do: log in with your id and password, be a responsible user and respect privacy, use the internet only when needed, inform parents or teachers if someone bullies you, keep antivirus updated and scan downloads, use public monitored chat rooms with an alias, shop only on secure sites, block people who make you uncomfortable. Don't: give personal information, share your user-id and password (change them regularly), tag friends in awkward photos, post objectionable content, spread rumours, be rude, meet an online friend alone, open attachments from unknown sources, or let the browser remember passwords.
